content: Menopause is defined as the cessation of menstrual cycles, typically occurring between the ages of 40 and 58 years. The symptoms of menopause vary widely among individuals, and there are no universally experienced symptoms. Studies have shown that Chinese, Japanese, African American, and Hispanic women report significantly fewer menopausal symptoms compared to Caucasian women. In Western societies, the most commonly reported symptoms include hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and sleep disturbances. Hot flushes can begin while a woman is still menstruating and tend to resolve within a few years after menopause for approximately two-thirds of women. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT), which involves the administration of estrogen alone or in combination with progestogen, is considered the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. A Cochrane review of randomized trials demonstrated a 75% reduction in hot flushes with hormone therapy, equating to 18 fewer episodes per week, compared to a 50% reduction with placebo. However, HRT is associated with significant risks. The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) studies revealed that both estrogen-only and combined estrogen-progestogen therapies were linked to an increased risk of stroke, deep vein thrombosis, and gallbladder disease. Additionally, combined therapy was associated with a higher incidence of breast cancer and dementia in women over the age of 65. Progestogens are a class of hormones that bind to progesterone receptors. This group includes both the natural female sex hormone progesterone and synthetic derivatives known as progestins. Progestogens are one of the five major classes of steroid hormones, alongside estrogens, androgens, mineralocorticoids, and glucocorticoids. Progesterone, the natural form, is named for its role in supporting pregnancy (pro-gestational), although it is also present during other phases of the menstrual and estrous cycles. Progestogens have diverse mechanisms of action and are used for a variety of medical purposes, including contraception, treatment of endometriosis, management of menstrual disorders, acne therapy, and alleviation of premenstrual syndrome. These hormones can be administered through various routes, including oral tablets, progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems, injections, vaginal pessaries, gels, creams, nasal sprays, and transdermal applications. Progestogens alone have been shown to effectively alleviate hot flushes. However, the precise mechanisms by which progestogens restore thermoregulatory function remain unclear. Similarly, the exact pathophysiology of hot flushes is not fully understood, though it is believed to involve an alteration in the hypothalamic set-point temperature. Both estrogens and progestogens are known to interact with multiple neurotransmitter systems. One hypothesis suggests that serotonin plays a role in the development of hot flushes, and the interaction of progestogens with the serotonergic system may contribute to their beneficial effects in reducing these symptoms. The WHI study results indicated that the use of estrogen during menopause, whether alone or combined with progestogen, resulted in more harm than benefit when compared to placebo. This underscores the need for alternative therapies that can provide relief from hot flushes with fewer associated risks. Progestogens, particularly depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, have not been shown to significantly increase the risk of venous thromboembolism, heart attack, or stroke. In contrast, the use of oral estrogen in women with a history of venous thromboembolism has been associated with an increased risk of recurrence. Progestogens may therefore represent a suitable alternative for women at high risk of thromboembolic disease or for those in whom estrogen therapy is contraindicated.
